reason: Gives a concrete test (ignore the tool, name the property lost) and flags the specific trap that encryption can be a control or a weapon, which is what unlocks ransomware -> Availability.

Poses two questions (noticed first vs. suffered unknowingly) without saying which one decides. Ransomware resolves by the first-noticed loss, silent payroll edits by the unnoticed one, so a novice can apply it either way and e.g. pull ransomware toward Confidentiality.

It mostly rewords the three bucket names as purposes, which 'primarily provides' already asks for. 'Holding less data in the first place' also describes Privacy too narrowly and could make after-the-fact erasure seem not to belong there.

'Sort by the reason it was put there' repeats hint 0 and the prompt's 'primarily'. It warns that overlap exists but gives no way to resolve it (e.g. signing vs. authentication, or an audit log's 'who').
Turns abstract type labels into one test, 'what does the enforcing?' (machine / people following a rule / physical barrier), which settles encryption and background checks directly.
Repeats the prompt's own instruction to ignore function (preventive/detective) and answer type. Nothing new for someone who read the prompt.

The prompt already gives the 'who' framing, and the 'who is protected?' test points Canon II items the wrong way. Not exaggerating protects the prospect (suggests III), and refusing an unauthorised scan protects the network owner (suggests I or III), when both are about your own honesty and legality.
Repeats the prompt's 'most directly about' instruction and gives no way to tell what a situation is fundamentally about.
Judging likelihood/impact and ranking are inside the same listed step, so the hint orders nothing between the five items. It only restates that step's internal logic.

Tells the learner that something remains after treatment and needs an owner, which places 'document residual risk and have it accepted' after treatment/apply rather than straight after choosing a treatment.

Gives an ordered decision tree (external? optional? then intention / requirement / sequence) that maps onto all five layers. Minor risk: 'Every system must have a named owner' reads as a specific requirement and could be pushed to Standard.

Read after hint 0, the force-and-specificity axes are already part of that tree, and this hint gives no mapping from the pair to a layer. 'Detailed and optional' also doesn't fit the vague passphrase guideline, which may confuse.
